To sequester means to isolate or separate something (or someone) from the rest, and keep it apart — usually for a specific purpose or by force.

Think of it like this: imagine picking one apple out of a basket and placing it in a separate box, away from all the others. You have sequestered that apple. The key ideas baked into this word are:

  • Separation — something is removed from its usual environment or group.
  • Deliberateness — it doesn't happen by accident. Someone or something causes the separation.
  • A reason behind it — the isolation serves a goal (safety, fairness, control, storage, etc.)

The same core idea — deliberate isolation — shows up in several different areas of life. Here they all are:

1. Isolating a Person or Group (General Use)

You can sequester a person or a group of people by cutting them off from the outside world.

"The scientists were sequestered in a remote research station for six months."

Here, the scientists are separated from society and kept in one place. They can't freely come and go.

"She sequestered herself in her room to study for the exam."

Notice here she chose to isolate herself. You can sequester yourself, meaning you voluntarily withdraw from the world around you. This is a slightly softer, more poetic use of the word.

2. Sequestering a Jury (Legal Use — People)

This is one of the most common places you'll hear this word, especially in news about big court trials.

When a jury is sequestered, the jurors are kept completely isolated from the public, from the news, and from outside information for the entire duration of the trial. They may be housed in a hotel, cut off from their phones, TV, and newspapers.

Why? Because the law wants jurors to decide the case only based on what they hear inside the courtroom — not based on news headlines, public opinion, or conversations with friends and family. Sequestering them protects the fairness of the trial.

"The judge decided to sequester the jury because the case was attracting enormous media attention."

3. Seizing or Holding Assets (Legal Use — Property)

In law, to sequester can also mean to take hold of someone's property — money, assets, or belongings — and keep it under legal control until a dispute is resolved.

Think of it as the law saying: "We're locking this away so nobody can touch it until we figure out who it rightfully belongs to, or until the person pays what they owe."

"The court sequestered the company's funds while the fraud investigation was ongoing."

The money hasn't been permanently taken away — it's just frozen and separated from the owner's control for the time being.

4. Carbon Sequestration (Scientific Use)

This is a hugely important use of the word in environmental science.

To sequester carbon means to capture carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the atmosphere and store it somewhere so it can't continue warming the planet.

Nature does this naturally — trees and plants absorb CO₂ and lock it inside their wood, roots, and soil. Oceans do it too. Scientists are also developing technologies that artificially pull CO₂ out of the air and pump it deep underground for long-term storage.

"Planting more forests is one of the most effective ways to sequester carbon."

The carbon is being separated from the atmosphere and stored away — the same core idea as always, just applied to chemistry and climate.

5. Budget Sequestration (Political/Government Use)

In government and politics — particularly in the United States — sequestration refers to a process where a set of government funds is automatically cut off or withheld from spending.

It's as if the government puts a portion of its budget in a locked box and says, "This money cannot be spent." This usually happens as a result of a law that forces automatic spending cuts when politicians fail to agree on a budget.

"The sequester led to automatic cuts across nearly every government department."

Again, the same idea: money is isolated, separated, and made unavailable.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Sequester" is a formal word. You won't typically hear it in casual everyday conversation. It belongs more in legal documents, news reporting, scientific writing, and formal speeches.

It also carries a sense of authority and control — someone in power (a judge, the law, nature, a government) is doing the separating. Even when a person sequesters themselves, there's a sense of strong, deliberate will behind the action.

Compared to simpler words like "isolate" or "separate," sequester sounds more official, more purposeful, and often implies that the separation will last for a defined period and serve a very specific function.
How It Differs from Similar Words

IdeaWhy "Sequester" Is Different

Isolate is the closest synonym. But "isolate" is neutral and general — you can isolate almost anything for almost any reason. "Sequester" implies more formality, more specific purpose, and often some kind of authority or official process behind the action.

Confiscate means to permanently take something away, usually as a punishment. Sequestering property is different — it's temporary and neutral (the property may be returned).

Quarantine means isolating something to prevent the spread of disease. Sequestering is broader — it isn't limited to health situations.

Withdraw means to pull back. You can withdraw yourself, but it doesn't carry the sense of being kept apart that sequester does.

No matter the context — a jury, carbon dioxide, government money, or a person — "sequester" always means the same thing at its core:

To deliberately separate and keep something away from its usual surroundings, for a specific and purposeful reason.

The thing being sequestered is removed, held apart, and kept that way — whether by a judge, a law, a scientific process, or personal choice.

Once you internalize that central idea — deliberate separation with purpose — every use of this word, in any field, will immediately make sense to you.
